frictionVectors.title: European gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains reliant on Algerian pipeline and LNG supplies, giving Algiers leverage but also exposing it to pressure over pricing, migration, and regional diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya complicates Algeria’s border security and diplomatic balancing while limiting regional infrastructure connectivity.

frictionVectors.title: External oil dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators, declining production, and debt-service obligations continue to constrain Luanda’s control over hydrocarbon revenues and investment decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor geopolitics
frictionVectors.details: U.S. and European backing for the corridor strengthens Angola’s strategic position but creates competing expectations around access to Congolese and Zambian critical minerals.

frictionVectors.title: Niger border and transit dispute
frictionVectors.details: Political tension with Niger has disrupted established trade routes and exposed Benin’s dependence on cross-border transport infrastructure and regional diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: Northern insurgency exposure
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity moving south from the Sahel threatens parks, roads, and agricultural zones, increasing reliance on foreign security assistance.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains strong negotiating leverage, but dependence on global diamond demand and its long relationship with De Beers remains a structural vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral diversification race
frictionVectors.details: New interest in copper, nickel, lithium, and rare earths could broaden sovereignty if processing develops domestically, but foreign capital remains essential.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector control struggle
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking tighter state oversight of gold production, but artisanal mining, smuggling, and insecurity continue to divert value beyond formal state channels.

frictionVectors.title: Security dependence on Russia
frictionVectors.details: Expanded Russian military cooperation reduces reliance on Western partners but creates new political, operational, and resource-governance dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Mining Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Gold, nickel and coltan projects attract foreign capital while limited transparency and weak processing capacity constrain Burundi's control over value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda Security Friction
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over armed groups and cross-border support keep the frontier politically volatile and complicate regional trade and infrastructure planning.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport and digital-connectivity development relies heavily on foreign lenders and strategic partners, creating long-term exposure to external commercial priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Energy Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported energy and tourism revenue leaves the archipelago sensitive to shipping disruptions, climate shocks and shifts in European demand.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Mining Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed investment around Kribi, iron ore and transport corridors is expanding export capacity, but domestic processing and contract transparency remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Conflict and Infrastructure Risk
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest threatens roads, plantations and energy infrastructure while weakening state control over productive regions.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security-Mining Nexus
frictionVectors.details: Russian security personnel and affiliated commercial networks retain significant influence, linking regime protection to access in gold and diamond-producing areas.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and Border Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country depends on external actors and neighboring corridors for security, fuel and trade, leaving resource exports vulnerable to conflict and political pressure.

highlights: Oil and gold remain strategic anchors

frictionVectors.title: Oil Revenue Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon income remains central to state finances, while foreign operators and transit infrastructure limit domestic control over pricing, technology and downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Spillover and External Security
frictionVectors.details: War in Sudan strains border security and humanitarian capacity, encouraging reliance on foreign military, financial and diplomatic partners.

frictionVectors.title: France–Comoros Territorial Tension
frictionVectors.details: France's administration of Mayotte remains the central sovereignty dispute, while migration controls and naval enforcement periodically strain bilateral relations.

frictionVectors.title: External Reliance for Connectivity
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic fiscal and infrastructure capacity leaves energy, telecommunications, and transport networks dependent on foreign financing and partners.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Backed Armed Groups
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and other armed groups continues to undermine state control in the east, threatening mining corridors and enabling cross-border mineral leakage.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Minerals Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt attract intense competition from Chinese, Western, and regional actors, while weak enforcement limits Kinshasa's ability to secure equitable value and supply-chain control.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: State finances and export earnings remain heavily exposed to oil production, foreign operators, and volatile global prices, constraining economic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, construction, and resource-linked projects expand connectivity but can increase debt exposure and external influence over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Sovereignty Gap
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan is strengthening domestic processing and producer oversight, but foreign traders, price volatility, and compliance costs still limit national control over cocoa value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Expansion of Abidjan and San Pedro ports attracts French, Chinese, and other external capital, while instability across the Sahel raises pressure on northern transport and security infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Footprint
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military presences generate revenue and leverage but constrain independent security policymaking and deepen great-power competition.

frictionVectors.title: Port Debt and Corridor Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's port economy is closely tied to Ethiopia and Chinese-linked infrastructure financing, leaving sovereignty vulnerable to debt pressures and shifts in regional trade flows.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked reforms and major Gulf investments provide liquidity but increase outside leverage over strategic assets, land, and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Nile security
frictionVectors.details: Attacks near the Red Sea threaten Suez revenues, while the GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains a central sovereignty and water-security concern.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil output and aging fields leave the state reliant on foreign operators, external technology, and volatile export revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction has expanded state infrastructure while increasing dependence on external finance and contractors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc projects provide hard currency but depend heavily on foreign capital, operators, and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's position near the Bab el-Mandeb attracts competing regional and external security interests, increasing pressure on its port and coastal policy.

frictionVectors.title: Regional economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Africa remains central to trade, energy access, finance, and logistics, limiting Eswatini's room for independent resource and infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and textile exposure
frictionVectors.details: Export industries remain vulnerable to foreign market preferences, trade-rule changes, and multinational supply-chain decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD gives Ethiopia greater control over its electricity and water infrastructure but continues to generate acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on external financing constrain policy space, while conflict and insecurity threaten transport, energy, and mining projects.

highlights: Junta converts transition into civilian rule
Oil and manganese remain strategic anchors

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The post-Bongo authorities are seeking greater state participation and transparency in oil, manganese, and infrastructure deals. This strengthens formal sovereignty but risks investor hesitation and contract disputes.

frictionVectors.title: French influence recalibration
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is reducing the political primacy of France while retaining commercial and security ties. Gulf, Chinese, and regional partners are competing for access to ports, minerals, and energy projects.

highlights: Senegal remains the indispensable external partner
Cashew, fisheries, and tourism face weak state leverage

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for trade routes, energy connectivity, food access, and security cooperation. This provides stability but constrains Banjul's room to diversify infrastructure and foreign partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries enforcement gap
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fleets and limited monitoring capacity continue to pressure coastal fish stocks and local livelihoods. Weak enforcement reduces the state's ability to capture the full value of its maritime resources.

highlights: Gold remains powerful but lithium strategy is unsettled

frictionVectors.title: External debt and conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF support have improved short-term stability but constrain spending and national control over economic policy. Fiscal pressure increases dependence on external creditors and commodity revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and critical minerals
frictionVectors.details: Illegal gold mining is degrading waterways and undermining state authority, while prospective lithium projects raise disputes over local value addition and ownership. Accra is pushing domestic processing but faces strong investor and creditor pressures.

highlights: Bauxite power is expanding through Simandou

frictionVectors.title: Simandou sovereignty contest
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore and rail-port complex is drawing major Chinese and international capital, giving Conakry leverage but also creating dependence on foreign operators and infrastructure finance. Local-content, revenue-sharing, and environmental concerns remain acute.

frictionVectors.title: Junta legitimacy and contracts
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities use mining projects to strengthen domestic legitimacy while delaying a return to civilian rule. Concentrated decision-making increases the risk of opaque concessions, sanctions exposure, and social unrest.

highlights: Cashew exports dominate a fragile economy

frictionVectors.title: Cashew-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign traders and processors capture much of the value from Guinea-Bissau's cashew economy, while weak regulation leaves farmers exposed to price swings. Limited domestic processing keeps the country dependent on external markets and logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Port and narcotics vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Bissau's weak institutions and limited maritime enforcement make the country vulnerable to transnational narcotics networks and politically connected smuggling. External security assistance can contain risks but also deepens dependence on outside actors.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Strategic Assets
frictionVectors.details: Heavy debt-service obligations constrain Nairobi's control over infrastructure priorities and increase dependence on IMF, Chinese, Gulf, and other external financiers. Ports, railways, energy, and digital networks remain central to sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and Northern Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Competing external interests around Lamu port, the Northern Corridor, and regional trade routes create pressure over security, land, and commercial access. Al-Shabaab insecurity further raises the cost of protecting strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide vital revenue but deepen dependence on Pretoria and expose Maseru to disputes over pricing, project delays, and compensation. Large construction contracts also create recurring concerns about foreign influence and corruption.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Economic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho relies heavily on South Africa for trade, electricity, and market access, limiting its bargaining autonomy. Political instability can further weaken oversight of water, mining, and infrastructure agreements.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Port Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, and other mineral projects remain dominated by foreign operators, with rail and port access tying national revenue to concession terms. The government faces pressure to renegotiate benefits without deterring investment or provoking arbitration.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Mining and Logging
frictionVectors.details: Informal gold mining and illicit timber extraction weaken state revenue and local land rights. Weak enforcement creates openings for foreign traders and politically connected intermediaries to capture value.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Oil Authorities
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to contest control over fields, export terminals, budgets, and the National Oil Corporation. Production remains vulnerable to blockades and bargaining by militias seeking direct access to oil rents.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military and Energy Footprints
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, Egypt, the UAE, and European states retain interests in Libya's security and energy sectors. Foreign bases, security partnerships, and offshore agreements constrain unified national control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Local Backlash
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects are largely foreign-financed and export-oriented, limiting domestic value capture. Land acquisition, water use, and environmental impacts continue to generate local resistance and political pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese and Gulf Commercial Expansion
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and other external investors are expanding their roles in mining, agriculture, ports, and infrastructure. Limited state capacity makes contract transparency and strategic oversight difficult.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Sovereign Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking foreign investment in uranium, rare earths, and other minerals while facing pressure to offer favorable terms. Limited fiscal capacity weakens the state's negotiating position over long-term resource control.

frictionVectors.title: Fuel and Power Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-exchange shortages and reliance on imported fuel continue to expose Malawi to external price and logistics shocks. Unreliable electricity also limits domestic value addition and increases dependence on donor-backed infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is asserting greater state participation and fiscal control over gold mining, creating tension with multinational operators. Production and export revenues remain vulnerable to insecurity, opaque arrangements, and informal networks.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Mali's reliance on Russian security personnel and political backing has reduced Western leverage but created a new dependency. The arrangement carries risks of opaque resource-linked transactions and limited accountability.

highlights: Iron and fisheries remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Greater Tortue Ahmeyim Gas Project
frictionVectors.details: The offshore gas project with Senegal offers Mauritania new revenue and diplomatic weight, but shared infrastructure and export governance require sustained bilateral coordination. Delays or cost pressures could reduce near-term fiscal gains.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Extractive Logistics
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, port infrastructure, and fisheries remain heavily linked to foreign operators and markets. Mauritania is gaining bargaining power but still has limited domestic processing capacity and exposure to commodity-price cycles.

highlights: Indian Ocean logistics gain strategic value

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Maritime Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius continues to pursue recognition of its sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago while managing the strategic realities of the Diego Garcia facility. The issue remains sensitive to relations with the United Kingdom, United States, and India.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Digital Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Indian, Chinese, Gulf, and Western actors compete for influence over Mauritius's port, finance, and digital connectivity sectors. The government retains comparatively strong regulatory capacity but must preserve neutrality among partners.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses phosphate, fisheries, renewable-energy, and infrastructure development in Western Sahara to consolidate territorial control. Recognition and investment decisions by external partners remain a continuing source of diplomatic friction.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence in Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is diversifying partnerships across Europe, the Gulf, China, and the United States in ports, energy, rail, and manufacturing. This strengthens resilience but creates competing external interests around supply chains and regional alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled LNG Security
frictionVectors.details: The LNG sector remains dependent on international operators, external financing, and foreign security support. Delays and security risks limit Mozambique's ability to convert gas wealth into sovereign fiscal gains.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent attacks continue to threaten roads, energy facilities, and coastal logistics in the north. Local grievances and weak state presence complicate both reconstruction and resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Oil Investment Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Namibia is attracting major foreign interest in uranium, offshore hydrocarbons, and critical minerals. The central challenge is securing local processing, jobs, and fiscal returns without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Energy Capacity Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Walvis Bay and planned hydrogen infrastructure are strategically important but require substantial external capital and grid expansion. Limited domestic industrial capacity could leave Namibia primarily an exporter of raw energy and minerals.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Disputes
frictionVectors.details: The military authorities are seeking greater state control and better terms from foreign mining interests. Administrative weakness, sanctions risk, and insecurity could still prevent the state from translating bargaining power into stable revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Attacks by jihadist groups threaten transport corridors, agricultural zones, and the country's oil-export infrastructure. Reduced Western involvement and deeper reliance on regional or non-Western partners create new security dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Dominated Energy Finance
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria is pursuing greater domestic value capture through refining and gas development, but upstream investment, technology, and financing remain heavily internationalized. Production losses, theft, and contract uncertainty weaken sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Grid Fragility
frictionVectors.details: Oil theft, sabotage, and unreliable power infrastructure continue to erode public revenues and industrial competitiveness. Security responses often remain fragmented across federal, state, and private actors.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral and Security Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's regional security posture and alleged links to mineral flows from eastern DRC generate sustained diplomatic pressure. Sanctions, border tensions, and reputational costs could constrain access to external capital and supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Investment Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The state exercises strong domestic control over infrastructure and development policy, but remains reliant on foreign aid, concessional finance, and investment. External partners retain leverage through budget support, trade access, and technology transfers.

frictionVectors.title: UNCERTAIN OFFSHORE EXPLORATION
frictionVectors.details: Interest in the jointly managed Nigeria–Sao Tome offshore zone has not translated into commercially viable production. Limited state capacity leaves the country dependent on foreign operators and partners for exploration, monitoring, and revenue assurance.

frictionVectors.title: GULF OF GUINEA SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Illegal fishing and maritime crime threaten fisheries and future offshore assets. Sao Tome relies heavily on external naval cooperation and donor-funded maritime surveillance.

frictionVectors.title: CONTRACT AND DEBT RENEGOTIATION
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater transparency and domestic value from hydrocarbon projects while facing tight fiscal constraints and international financing conditions. Renegotiation risks delaying investment or triggering disputes with foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND ENERGY INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing, coastal degradation, and foreign access agreements remain politically sensitive. Gas revenues will depend on reliable transport, power, and processing infrastructure that still requires substantial external capital.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL FINANCE AND ASSET OWNERSHIP
frictionVectors.details: Tourism, fisheries, and infrastructure depend heavily on foreign investment and imported inputs. Debt sustainability and concessions can narrow the government's room to control strategic assets despite relatively strong institutions.

frictionVectors.title: INDIAN OCEAN SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles must balance cooperation with India, France, China, and other maritime partners. Foreign naval access and surveillance support improve security but create sensitivities over neutrality and control of the exclusive economic zone.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONCESSION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, bauxite, and gold projects remain reliant on foreign capital, technology, and export logistics. The state is seeking stronger revenue capture and domestic processing, but bargaining power is constrained by infrastructure and financing needs.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, road, and mining logistics projects can improve connectivity while tying strategic infrastructure to external commercial interests. Weak fiscal space limits the government's ability to fund alternatives or enforce long-term local-content goals.

highlights: Federal control over resources remains contested
External security partnerships shape the coastline

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE OIL AND FEDERAL DISPUTES
frictionVectors.details: Interest from foreign energy companies and Turkey has revived offshore ambitions, but disagreements between the federal government and member states over licensing and revenue sharing remain unresolved. Weak regulatory capacity raises the risk of opaque deals and limited national benefit.

frictionVectors.title: PORTS, BASES, AND MARITIME CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states, the United States, and other partners provide security and port-related support, but their competing interests complicate sovereign control of coastal infrastructure. Al-Shabaab, piracy risks, and fragmented authority continue to restrict effective management of Somalia's maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CAPITAL AND PROCESSING CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Foreign and domestic mining interests retain strong influence over platinum, manganese and chromium supply chains. Pretoria is pressing for local beneficiation, but infrastructure and investment constraints limit leverage.

frictionVectors.title: POWER AND FREIGHT INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Eskom reliability and rail-port congestion continue to weaken state control over mineral exports. Private-sector participation is expanding, but raises concerns over strategic infrastructure governance.

frictionVectors.title: SUDAN PIPELINE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on export infrastructure crossing war-affected Sudan, leaving production exposed to sabotage, blockades and bargaining by external and domestic armed actors.

frictionVectors.title: OIL REVENUE AND SECURITY NETWORKS
frictionVectors.details: Opaque oil arrangements and competition among political elites, neighboring states and international contractors constrain sovereign control of revenues. Fiscal dependence on hydrocarbons limits diversification.

highlights: Gold and ports attract rival patrons

frictionVectors.title: GOLD ECONOMY AND EXTERNAL SPONSORS
frictionVectors.details: Gold flows finance competing armed networks and draw involvement from regional traders and foreign patrons. The conflict has sharply reduced civilian oversight of the country's most liquid strategic resource.

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA PORT COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan and prospective Red Sea infrastructure has become strategically important to Gulf, Russian and regional actors. Wartime dependence on external logistics and security partners erodes national bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: LNG DEVELOPMENT AND CONTRACT TERMS
frictionVectors.details: Negotiations over the long-delayed offshore gas project continue to test Tanzania's demands for fiscal value, local content and regulatory control against pressure for investor certainty.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAILWAY INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf and other foreign-backed infrastructure interests are increasing competition around Dar es Salaam and regional corridors. Diversification of partners improves Tanzania's leverage but complicates strategic oversight.

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCE AND FOREIGN CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is a major regional gateway, but its expansion depends heavily on foreign operators, lenders and shipping networks. This creates exposure to external commercial and geopolitical pressure.

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE SECTOR GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Phosphates remain strategically important, yet production challenges and limited downstream processing constrain domestic value capture. Foreign technical and investment partnerships remain influential.

frictionVectors.title: IMF-EU Financing Tension
frictionVectors.details: Tunis is resisting politically costly external reform conditions while relying on European financial and migration cooperation. Fiscal stress limits its room to protect strategic assets and negotiate independently.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Phosphate Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Declining domestic energy security and disruptions in phosphate production weaken export earnings. Foreign investment and European energy ties are increasingly important to maintaining economic stability.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sanctions Risk
frictionVectors.details: The oil pipeline remains central to Uganda's resource strategy but depends on foreign operators, lenders, and regional infrastructure. European criticism over environmental and human-rights concerns continues to raise financing and reputational risks.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese contractors and lenders remain influential in transport, energy, and extractive infrastructure. Kampala gains delivery capacity but faces concentrated exposure to external creditors and project partners.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Copper Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking greater local processing, revenue capture, and strategic influence over copper and cobalt while major foreign firms retain substantial operational power. Competition among Chinese, Western, and Gulf investors gives Lusaka leverage but also intensifies bargaining pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Power Supply Constraint
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages undermine mining output and industrial sovereignty, increasing reliance on regional imports and emergency generation. Climate-linked hydropower volatility makes the energy bottleneck structurally persistent.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and Platinum Concession Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is using export controls and beneficiation requirements to retain more value from lithium, platinum, and other minerals, but Chinese and other foreign investors still dominate capital, technology, and market access. Weak institutions reduce the state's ability to enforce favorable terms consistently.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions, Debt, and Infrastructure Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, arrears, and limited access to concessional finance push Harare toward narrower partnerships, particularly with China and other non-Western actors. This preserves project financing options while increasing dependence on politically aligned external creditors.
